entries.title: Is our simulation engine a faithful copy of the published one?
entries.question: Does our engine give the same answers as the 2024 study's own code on the same brain and the same input?
entries.why: Every later result depends on the engine. If it differed from the published model, a match or a miss would tell us about our code, not about the fly.
entries.brain: FlyWire, the wiring released with the 2024 study.
method: Sugar-taste neurons switched on at 100 signals per second.
Run in our engine and in the published code; compare the tongue neuron (MN9) and the 200 most active neurons.
entries.rule: No pass mark was set in advance; this is a direct side-by-side comparison.

results.label: MN9 (one copy): 66.6 vs 67.0 firings per second (ours vs published)
MN9 (other copy): 49.5 vs 48.6
Neurons that fired: 413 vs 404
Firing of the 200 most active neurons: correlation 0.999 (1 = identical)

entries.conclusion: The two engines agree closely. One detail had to be matched exactly: input arriving while a neuron is recovering from a spike is lost, as in the published code.
entries.confidence: High: the comparison is direct, on identical inputs.

discovery.text: None. This is a check of our tools.

entries.title: Does sugar make the simulated fly stick out its tongue?
entries.question: Before any experiment: does the FlyWire brain reproduce the best-established taste results in real flies?
entries.why: If the brain can't get known results right, its predictions mean nothing. Passing is required before any experiment is reported.
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Switch on the sugar-taste neurons at 8 strengths (10 to 200 signals per second), bitter neurons, water neurons, and combinations.
Read MN9, the motor neuron that extends the proboscis (tongue).
30 repeats of 1 simulated second per condition.
entries.rule: All of: C1. Sugar at 100 signals per second makes MN9 fire 10 or more times per second; C2. More sugar, more MN9 firing (from 10 to 200 signals per second); C3. Bitter alone does not make MN9 fire; C4. Bitter cuts the sugar response at least in half; C5. Water also makes MN9 fire; C6. Activity stays contained: fewer than 2,000 neurons fire. C1-C4 and C6 must pass.

results.label: C1. Sugar at 100 signals per second makes MN9 fire 10 or more times per second
C2. More sugar, more MN9 firing (from 10 to 200 signals per second)
C3. Bitter alone does not make MN9 fire
C4. Bitter cuts the sugar response at least in half
C5. Water also makes MN9 fire
C6. Activity stays contained: fewer than 2,000 neurons fire
MN9 to sugar 100: 61.4/s; bitter alone: 0.0/s; sugar + bitter: 0.1/s; water: 31.2/s
Sugar-response curve rises steadily (rank correlation 0.994)

entries.conclusion: Passed all six rules. Every experiment in the lab runs on this brain.
entries.confidence: High for these basic taste results: they are large, clear effects.

discovery.text: Reproduces known results (by design). No new claim.

entries.title: Does bitter beat even strong sugar?
entries.question: Does bitter beat even strong sugar?
entries.why: This result was found in living flies. Checking whether the untouched simulated brain reproduces it measures how far to trust its new predictions.
entries.real: Activating bitter neurons stopped proboscis extension to weak sugar (50 mM sucrose) and stopped drinking even of strong sugar (1 M). (Shiu et al. 2024, optogenetics)
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Weak sugar = the lowest calibration rate at which MN9 fires 10+ per second on this brain (decided by rule, read from the calibration run). Strong sugar = 200 per second. Bitter, Ir94e and water = 200 per second. Activated single cell types = 100 per second. Silencing = all connections to and from the neuron set to zero (as in the published code).
entries.rule: Bitter cuts MN9 firing by at least half for weak sugar AND for strong sugar.

results.label: Weak sugar (60/s): MN9 28.9 → 0.0 with bitter
Strong sugar (200/s): MN9 89.0 → 12.4 with bitter

discovery.text: Reproduces a known real-fly result. No new claim.

entries.title: Ir94e: a brake that only works on weak sugar
entries.question: Ir94e: a brake that only works on weak sugar
entries.why: This result was found in living flies. Checking whether the untouched simulated brain reproduces it measures how far to trust its new predictions.
entries.real: Activating Ir94e taste neurons reduced proboscis extension to weak sugar (50 mM) but failed to stop it for strong sugar (1 M). (Shiu et al. 2024, optogenetics)
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Weak sugar = the lowest calibration rate at which MN9 fires 10+ per second on this brain (decided by rule, read from the calibration run). Strong sugar = 200 per second. Bitter, Ir94e and water = 200 per second. Activated single cell types = 100 per second. Silencing = all connections to and from the neuron set to zero (as in the published code).
entries.rule: Ir94e cuts MN9 by at least half for weak sugar, AND MN9 keeps at least a quarter of its sugar-only firing for strong sugar.

results.label: Weak sugar: MN9 28.9 → 0.1 with Ir94e (needs a cut of half or more)
Strong sugar: MN9 89.0 → 53.4 with Ir94e (needs to keep a quarter or more)

entries.conclusion: Matched 2 of 2. Caution: switching on Ir94e at this strength set off a chain reaction (8,844 and 8,839 neurons fired, against 377 for weak sugar alone). The answer matches real flies, but it comes from a brain-wide surge, so we don't treat it as strong evidence.
entries.confidence: Low: the match comes from a brain-wide surge, so it is weak evidence.

discovery.text: Reproduces a known real-fly result. No new claim.

entries.title: Usnea: water neuron or sugar neuron?
entries.question: Usnea: water neuron or sugar neuron?
entries.why: This result was found in living flies. Checking whether the untouched simulated brain reproduces it measures how far to trust its new predictions.
entries.real: Usnea responds to water but not to sugar (calcium imaging). The 2024 study reports its own model got this wrong. (Shiu et al. 2024 (citing earlier imaging))
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Weak sugar = the lowest calibration rate at which MN9 fires 10+ per second on this brain (decided by rule, read from the calibration run). Strong sugar = 200 per second. Bitter, Ir94e and water = 200 per second. Activated single cell types = 100 per second. Silencing = all connections to and from the neuron set to zero (as in the published code).
entries.rule: Usnea fires 5+ per second for water AND under 1 per second for sugar (100 per second).

results.label: Usnea to water: 110.5/s (needs 5+)
Usnea to sugar: 72.6/s (needs under 1)

entries.conclusion: Matched 1 of 2. The original 2024 model made the same mistake, so this is a limit of the model, not of our copy of it. Something that stops Usnea responding to sugar in real flies isn't in the wiring-only model.
entries.confidence: The miss is clear and matches a miss the 2024 study reported for its own model.

discovery.text: Partly reproduces a known result; the miss points to something the wiring alone doesn't explain.

entries.title: Which neurons does water drinking need?
entries.question: Which neurons does water drinking need?
entries.why: This result was found in living flies. Checking whether the untouched simulated brain reproduces it measures how far to trust its new predictions.
entries.real: Silencing Usnea, Bract or Roundup reduced proboscis extension to water; silencing G2N-1 did not. (Shiu et al. 2024, optogenetic silencing (GtACR1))
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Weak sugar = the lowest calibration rate at which MN9 fires 10+ per second on this brain (decided by rule, read from the calibration run). Strong sugar = 200 per second. Bitter, Ir94e and water = 200 per second. Activated single cell types = 100 per second. Silencing = all connections to and from the neuron set to zero (as in the published code).
entries.rule: Using the study's own threshold: a neuron is 'needed' if silencing it lowers MN9's response to water by more than 20%. Pass for each neuron if the model's answer matches the real one (Usnea, Bract, Roundup: needed; G2N-1: not needed). Scored separately.

results.label: Usnea silenced: MN9 to water 31.7 → 45.3 (43% higher). Real fly: needed; model: not needed
Bract silenced: MN9 to water 31.7 → 19.2 (39% lower). Real fly: needed; model: needed
Roundup silenced: MN9 to water 31.7 → 0.3 (99% lower). Real fly: needed; model: needed
G2N-1 silenced: MN9 to water 31.7 → 23.7 (25% lower). Real fly: not needed; model: needed

entries.conclusion: Matched 2 of 4. Bract and Roundup match. Usnea and G2N-1 go the wrong way, the same two the 2024 study reported as surprises for its model.
entries.confidence: The miss is clear and matches a miss the 2024 study reported for its own model.

discovery.text: Partly reproduces a known result; the miss points to something the wiring alone doesn't explain.

entries.title: Antenna touch: which sensors trigger grooming?
entries.question: Antenna touch: which sensors trigger grooming?
entries.why: This result was found in living flies. Checking whether the untouched simulated brain reproduces it measures how far to trust its new predictions.
entries.real: Activating Johnston's organ neurons of type JO-CE strongly activated the grooming neuron aBN1; JO-F neurons did not, despite having almost as many synapses onto it. (Shiu et al. 2024, optogenetics + calcium imaging)
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: Weak sugar = the lowest calibration rate at which MN9 fires 10+ per second on this brain (decided by rule, read from the calibration run). Strong sugar = 200 per second. Bitter, Ir94e and water = 200 per second. Activated single cell types = 100 per second. Silencing = all connections to and from the neuron set to zero (as in the published code).
entries.rule: JO-CE (100 per second) makes aBN1 fire 5+ per second, AND JO-F (100 per second) leaves aBN1 under 1 per second. Scored separately.

results.label: JO-CE switched on → aBN1 26.0/s (needs 5+)
JO-F switched on → aBN1 0.9/s (needs under 1)

entries.conclusion: Matched 2 of 2. JO-F gave aBN1 0.9 firings per second: just under the line of 1. It counts as a match by the saved rule, but it's a close call.

entries.title: The Taste Bench: every combination of sugar, bitter and water
entries.question: What does the calibrated brain do for each mix of tastes?
entries.why: So anyone can see the brain respond, with real recorded runs rather than animations.
entries.brain: FlyWire v783 (female brain), wiring as published with the 2024 study's code (Connectivity_783: all synapses), published settings unchanged (w_syn 0.275 mV, 30 repeats x 1 s). This is the same brain the Fly Atlas shows in 3D.
method: 24 combinations: sugar none/50/100/200, bitter none/100/200, water none/200 signals per second.
10 repeats each; MN9 firing and every neuron that fired are recorded.
entries.rule: No pass mark: this is a demonstration of the calibrated brain, not a test.

results.label: Sugar 100: MN9 65.0/s (tongue out)
Sugar 100 + bitter 200: MN9 0.1/s (tongue stays in)
Sugar 100 + water 200: MN9 83.4/s (signals add up)

entries.conclusion: Bitter overrules sugar, and sugar and water add up, consistent with the calibration test.

discovery.text: None. A way to explore the calibrated brain.

entries.title: Discovery Screen 1: which neurons does the fly need to eat and to drink?
entries.question: If one neuron is switched off, can the fly still eat (sugar) or drink (water)?
entries.why: Most of these neurons have never been switched off in a living fly. The simulation can point a real lab to the few worth testing.
entries.brain: FlyWire v783, published wiring and settings (same as round 1; engine v2 only adds a record of spike times, the maths is unchanged).
method: The 200 most active neurons when sugar neurons fire at 100/s plus the 200 most active when water neurons fire at 200/s (from the round 1 records), leaving out the sugar and water sensors themselves and MN9: 286 neurons.

Silence each candidate on its own (all its outgoing connections set to zero, as in the published code) and run sugar 100/s, then water 200/s. 10 repeats each for the screen. Every neuron scored 'needed' is then re-run with 30 repeats, and only the 30-repeat result is reported.
entries.rule: A neuron is 'needed' for eating (or drinking) if silencing it lowers MN9's firing by more than 20% compared with the unsilenced run with the same repeats (the 2024 study's threshold). Each predicted neuron is marked 'tested in the 2024 study' if it appears in that study's named neuron lists, otherwise 'no living-fly test known to us'. We do not claim no one has ever tested it.

results.label: 286 neurons switched off one at a time; 8 predicted needed (confirmed with 30 repeats).
"Roundup" #1: eating 35% lower · Moderate lead
"Roundup" #2: eating 27% lower, drinking 98% lower · Strong lead
CB0192 #2: drinking 41% lower · Moderate lead
CB0051: drinking 55% lower · Strong lead
"Rattle": drinking 30% lower · Moderate lead
"Bract": drinking 34% lower · Moderate lead
CB0501: drinking 43% lower · Moderate lead
"Clavicle": drinking 84% lower · Strong lead

entries.conclusion: 8 neurons predicted needed: 7 for drinking, 2 for eating (Roundup #2 for both). For most neurons the signal finds another route, so the feeding circuit has backups.
entries.confidence: On known single-neuron silencing results, the model matched 2 of 4 when whole cell types were silenced (round 1, E6) and 3 of 4 one cell at a time in this screen (G2N-1 only just). Even a strong lead is a hypothesis.

confidence_rule.written: 2026-11-03, after the screen; it labels results and changes none of them
confidence_rule.sim: Clear in the simulation if the 95% range of the drop (from 30 paired runs) stays above the 20% "needed" line.
confidence_rule.size: Large effect if the drop is 50% or more; moderate if 20-50%.

levels.1: Weak lead: the 95% range dips below the 20% line

confidence_rule.track: On known single-neuron silencing results, the model matched 2 of 4 when whole cell types were silenced (round 1, E6) and 3 of 4 one cell at a time in this screen (G2N-1 only just). Even a strong lead is a hypothesis.

discovery.text: Potential discovery: 3 predictions (CB0192 #2, CB0051, CB0501) about neurons with no real-fly test known to us. They need a living-fly experiment to become a discovery.
